claim: Single-cell RNA-seq analysis of E10.5 mouse mandibular arch obtained high quality transcriptome profiles of 10,586 cells expressing 17,074 unique genes.
source: After filtering at both cell and gene levels using highly stringent criteria (see Materials and methods), we obtained high quality transcriptome profiles of 10,586 cells, which expressed 17,074 unique genes, with the median number of detected genes and transcripts at 2624 and 8824, respectively.
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental data obtained from scRNA-seq analysis with specific quantitative results.

claim: The majority of cells in the E10.5 mandibular arch were of neural crest origin, accounting for over 9000 of the 10,586 cells.
source: As expected, the majority of the cells were of neural crest origin, accounting for over 9000 of the 10,586 cells and are distributed in two subgroups, NC1 and NC2, representing cells in the proximal (expressing Barx1) and distal (expressing Hand2) regions of the E10.5 mandibular arch, respectively.
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative cell counts from the scRNA-seq analysis.

claim: Neural crest cells in the E10.5 mandibular arch are distributed in two subgroups, NC1 and NC2, representing cells in the proximal and distal regions respectively.
source: As expected, the majority of the cells were of neural crest origin, accounting for over 9000 of the 10,586 cells and are distributed in two subgroups, NC1 and NC2, representing cells in the proximal (expressing Barx1) and distal (expressing Hand2) regions of the E10.5 mandibular arch, respectively.
evidence: The manuscript describes clustering results from scRNA-seq data analysis.

claim: About 8% of the cells in the E10.5 mandibular arch were epithelial cells marked by Epcam expression.
source: About 8% of the cells were epithelial cells, which are marked by expression of Epcam (830 cells, including both endoderm and ectoderm cells).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative cell type distribution from scRNA-seq analysis.

claim: The NC3 cluster consisted of 484 cells distinguished by overall lower levels of transcripts and dramatically lower number of genes detected per cell.
source: The NC3 cluster, consisting of 484 cells, is distinguished from the other clusters primarily by overall lower levels of transcripts and dramatically lower number of genes detected per cell (Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and Figure 1—figure supplement 3, and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The manuscript describes quantitative characteristics of a cell cluster with reference to supporting figures.

claim: The NC3 cluster showed very low levels or absence of several ubiquitously expressed nuclear localized long noncoding RNAs including Malat1, Xist, Meg3, and Kcnq1ot1.
source: In addition, the NC3 cluster cells showed very low levels or absence of several ubiquitously expressed, nuclear localized long noncoding RNAs, including Malat1, Xist, Meg3, and Kcnq1ot1 (Supplementary file 2, Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The manuscript reports gene expression patterns observed in scRNA-seq data with reference to supporting figures.

claim: The NC3 cluster most likely resulted from incomplete lysis of a subset of single cells.
source: These data suggest that the NC3 cluster resulted, most likely, from incomplete lysis of a subset of single cells.
evidence: The manuscript provides an interpretation based on the observed data patterns.

claim: Iterative clustering analysis grouped mandibular neural crest mesenchyme cells into six subgroups.
source: We performed iterative clustering analysis of the neural crest cell populations from NC1 and NC2 clusters shown in Figure 1A, which further grouped the neural crest-derived mandibular mesenchyme cells into six subgroups.
evidence: The manuscript describes the computational analysis results with reference to figures.

claim: Subgroups 0 and 1 share high levels of expression of Hand2, a marker of the distal domain of the mandibular arch mesenchyme.
source: Subgroups 0 and 1 share high levels of expression of Hand2, a marker of the distal domain of the mandibular arch mesenchyme at this developmental stage, whereas Subgroup 2 lacks Hand2 expression and instead expresses the proximal domain marker genes Emx2 and Pou3f3 at high levels (Figure 1C).
evidence: The manuscript reports gene expression patterns from scRNA-seq data with reference to figures.

claim: Subgroup 2 lacks Hand2 expression and instead expresses the proximal domain marker genes Emx2 and Pou3f3 at high levels.
source: Subgroups 0 and 1 share high levels of expression of Hand2, a marker of the distal domain of the mandibular arch mesenchyme at this developmental stage, whereas Subgroup 2 lacks Hand2 expression and instead expresses the proximal domain marker genes Emx2 and Pou3f3 at high levels (Figure 1C).
evidence: The manuscript reports gene expression patterns from scRNA-seq data with reference to figures.

claim: Subgroup 3 expresses high levels of the caudal domain marker gene Gsc.
source: Subgroups 3 and 4 appear to distribute along the rostral-caudal axis, with Subgroup 3 expressing high levels of the caudal domain marker gene Gsc and with Subgroup 4 expressing high levels of the rostral domain marker genes Lhx8 and Lhx6 (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: The manuscript reports gene expression patterns from scRNA-seq data with reference to figures.

claim: Subgroup 4 expresses high levels of the rostral domain marker genes Lhx8 and Lhx6.
source: Subgroups 3 and 4 appear to distribute along the rostral-caudal axis, with Subgroup 3 expressing high levels of the caudal domain marker gene Gsc and with Subgroup 4 expressing high levels of the rostral domain marker genes Lhx8 and Lhx6 (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: The manuscript reports gene expression patterns from scRNA-seq data with reference to figures.

claim: Subgroup 5 cells are uniquely marked by high levels of expression of Notch2.
source: Subgroup 5 cells are more scattered than the other subgroups in the tSNE plot but are uniquely marked by high levels of expression of Notch2 (Figure 1B,C, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The manuscript reports gene expression patterns from scRNA-seq data with reference to figures and supplementary files.

claim: The cellular distributions in the tSNE plot correlated well with their spatial patterns of gene expression along the proximal-distal and rostral-caudal axes of the mandibular arch in the intact embryo.
source: Nevertheless, the cellular distributions in the tSNE plot correlated well with their spatial patterns of gene expression along the proximal-distal and rostral-caudal axes of the mandibular arch in the intact embryo (Figure 2).
evidence: The manuscript describes correlation between computational analysis and spatial expression patterns with reference to figures.

claim: Several Hedgehog signaling target genes, including Ptch1, Foxf1, and Foxf2, were among the top marker genes for Subgroup 0.
source: Strikingly, several Hedgehog signaling target genes, including Ptch1, Foxf1, and Foxf2, were among the top marker genes for Subgroup 0 whereas several BMP signaling target genes, including Msx1, Msx2, and Bambi were among the top markers for Subgroup 1.
evidence: The manuscript reports differential gene expression patterns from scRNA-seq analysis.

claim: Several BMP signaling target genes, including Msx1, Msx2, and Bambi, were among the top markers for Subgroup 1.
source: Strikingly, several Hedgehog signaling target genes, including Ptch1, Foxf1, and Foxf2, were among the top marker genes for Subgroup 0 whereas several BMP signaling target genes, including Msx1, Msx2, and Bambi were among the top markers for Subgroup 1.
evidence: The manuscript reports differential gene expression patterns from scRNA-seq analysis.

claim: Gene ontology analyses showed 'skeletal system development', 'ossification', and 'osteoblastic differentiation' among the enriched biological processes for both Subgroups 0 and 1.
source: Furthermore, gene ontology analyses showed 'skeletal system development', 'ossification', and 'osteoblastic differentiation' among the enriched biological processes for both Subgroups 0 and 1 (Supplementary file 4 and 5).
evidence: The manuscript reports results from gene ontology analysis with reference to supplementary files.

claim: Shh mRNA expression in the mandibular arch epithelium is restricted to the oropharyngeal side at E10.5.
source: Consistent with previous reports from studies of chick embryos (Brito et al., 2008; Haworth et al., 2007), we found that Shh mRNA expression in the mandibular arch epithelium is restricted to the oropharyngeal side at E10.5 (Figure 3E and E').
evidence: The manuscript reports in situ hybridization results with reference to figures and cites previous studies.

claim: Expression of Ptch1, Foxf1, and Foxf2 is restricted to the oropharyngeal side of the mandibular arch cells underneath the Shh-expressing epithelium.
source: Corresponding to this restricted Shh expression pattern, expression of Ptch1, Foxf1, and Foxf2, known transcriptional target genes of hedgehog signaling (Hoffmann et al., 2014; Jeong et al., 2004), is restricted to the oropharyngeal side of the mandibular arch cells underneath the Shh-expressing epithelium (Figure 3F–H and Figure 3F'–H').
evidence: The manuscript reports in situ hybridization and immunofluorescence results with reference to figures and cites previous studies.

claim: Bmp4 and Fgf8 mRNAs are expressed in the distal and proximal regions of the oral ectoderm respectively.
source: Whereas Bmp4 and Fgf8 mRNAs are expressed in the distal and proximal regions of the oral ectoderm (Figure 3I,I', M,M', N,N'), respectively, the down-stream target genes of BMP signaling, including Msx1, Msx2 and Alx4, are expressed in an aboral-to-oropharyngeal gradient pattern complementary to that of Foxf1 and Foxf2 in the distal mandibular arch mesenchyme (Figure 3J–L, and Figure 3J'–L', compare with Figure 3G'–H').
evidence: The manuscript reports in situ hybridization results with reference to figures.

claim: The downstream target genes of BMP signaling, including Msx1, Msx2 and Alx4, are expressed in an aboral-to-oropharyngeal gradient pattern complementary to that of Foxf1 and Foxf2 in the distal mandibular arch mesenchyme.
source: Whereas Bmp4 and Fgf8 mRNAs are expressed in the distal and proximal regions of the oral ectoderm (Figure 3I,I', M,M', N,N'), respectively, the down-stream target genes of BMP signaling, including Msx1, Msx2 and Alx4, are expressed in an aboral-to-oropharyngeal gradient pattern complementary to that of Foxf1 and Foxf2 in the distal mandibular arch mesenchyme (Figure 3J–L, and Figure 3J'–L', compare with Figure 3G'–H').
evidence: The manuscript reports in situ hybridization results with reference to figures.

claim: Lhx8 and Lhx6 mRNAs are expressed in a limited region of the rostral mandibular mesenchyme underlying the Fgf8 expressing epithelium.
source: In contrast, the Lhx8 and Lhx6 mRNAs are expressed in a limited region of the rostral mandibular mesenchyme underlying the Fgf8 expressing epithelium (Figure 3O–P and Figure 3O'–P').
evidence: The manuscript reports in situ hybridization results with reference to figures.

claim: The rostral-caudal axis of the mandibular arch mesenchyme along which the Fgf8-Lhx6/8 pathway is activated is distinct from the oral-aboral axis along which the Hedgehog and BMP signaling pathways exhibit complementary activity.
source: These results demonstrate clearly that the rostral-caudal axis of the mandibular arch mesenchyme along which the Fgf8-Lhx6/8 pathway is activated is distinct from the oral-aboral axis along which the Hedgehog and BMP signaling pathways exhibit complementary activity in the mandibular arch mesenchyme.
evidence: The manuscript provides an interpretation of the observed gene expression patterns.

claim: Smoc/c;Wnt1-Cre mice die perinatally and exhibit severe truncation of facial structures, including the maxilla and mandible.
source: Similar to the phenotype of Smoc/n;Wnt1-Cre mice (Smon is a Smo-null allele) as previously reported (Jeong et al., 2004), the Smoc/c;Wnt1-Cre mice die perinatally and exhibit severe truncation of facial structures, including the maxilla and mandible (Figure 4A–B), and agenesis of the oral tongue tissues (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports phenotypic observations from mutant mice with reference to figures and cites previous studies.

claim: Smoc/c;Wnt1-Cre mice exhibit agenesis of the oral tongue tissues.
source: Similar to the phenotype of Smoc/n;Wnt1-Cre mice (Smon is a Smo-null allele) as previously reported (Jeong et al., 2004), the Smoc/c;Wnt1-Cre mice die perinatally and exhibit severe truncation of facial structures, including the maxilla and mandible (Figure 4A–B), and agenesis of the oral tongue tissues (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports phenotypic observations from mutant mice with reference to figures and cites previous studies.

claim: Smoc/c;Wnt1-Cre mutants had mirror-image duplication of the dentary bone, including duplication of the condylar process.
source: Examination of the mandibular skeleton in E18.5 mouse embryos showed that the Smoc/c;Wnt1-Cre mutants had mirror-image duplication of the dentary bone, including duplication of the condylar process, although the mandibular skeleton is distally truncated (Figure 4C–D).
evidence: The manuscript reports skeletal analysis results from mutant mice with reference to figures.

claim: Smoc/c;Wnt1-Cre embryos had ectopic ossification in the oral side of the mandibular mesenchyme where the tongue failed to form.
source: We analyzed coronal sections of E13.5 Smoc/c;Wnt1-Cre embryos and their littermates and found that the Smoc/c;Wnt1-Cre embryos had ectopic ossification in the oral side of the mandibular mesenchyme where the tongue failed to form, as indicated by ectopic expression of Runx2 and alkaline phosphatase in the oral side of the mandibular mesenchyme (Figure 4E–H).
evidence: The manuscript reports histological analysis results from mutant mice with reference to figures.

claim: Hedgehog signaling in the neural crest cells is required for proper specification of the oral side of the mandibular mesenchyme.
source: These results suggest that hedgehog signaling in the neural crest cells is required for proper specification of the oral side of the mandibular mesenchyme.
evidence: The manuscript provides an interpretation of the observed phenotypes in mutant mice.

claim: Expression of Msx1, Msx2, and Alx4 mRNAs were all expanded to the oropharyngeal side of the distal mandibular arch mesenchyme in the Smoc/c;Wnt1-Cre mutant embryos by E10.5.
source: We compared the patterns of expression of the BMP target genes Msx1, Msx2, and Alx4 in the Smoc/c;Wnt1-Cre mutant embryos and their control littermates. We found that expression of Msx1, Msx2, and Alx4 mRNAs were all expanded to the oropharyngeal side of the distal mandibular arch mesenchyme in the Smoc/c;Wnt1-Cre mutant embryos by E10.5 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), suggesting that hedgehog signaling might specify oral fate of the mandibular mesenchyme through antagonizing BMP signaling.
evidence: The manuscript reports in situ hybridization results from mutant mice with reference to figures.

claim: Hedgehog signaling might specify oral fate of the mandibular mesenchyme through antagonizing BMP signaling.
source: We compared the patterns of expression of the BMP target genes Msx1, Msx2, and Alx4 in the Smoc/c;Wnt1-Cre mutant embryos and their control littermates. We found that expression of Msx1, Msx2, and Alx4 mRNAs were all expanded to the oropharyngeal side of the distal mandibular arch mesenchyme in the Smoc/c;Wnt1-Cre mutant embryos by E10.5 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), suggesting that hedgehog signaling might specify oral fate of the mandibular mesenchyme through antagonizing BMP signaling.
evidence: The manuscript provides a speculative interpretation of the observed gene expression changes.

claim: Smoc/n;Wnt1-Cre mouse embryos had significantly increased apoptosis of neural-crest derived facial mesenchyme, including mandibular arch mesenchyme at E9.5 to E10.5.
source: It has been reported that the Smoc/n;Wnt1-Cre mouse embryos had significantly increased apoptosis of neural-crest derived facial mesenchyme, including mandibular arch mesenchyme at E9.5 to E10.5 (Jeong et al., 2004).
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study reporting apoptosis in mutant mice.

claim: Cre expressed from the Hand2-Cre transgene is activated in post-migratory neural crest cells in the distal halves of the mandibular and other pharyngeal arches.
source: To investigate further whether hedgehog signaling plays a direct role in oral-aboral patterning of the mandibular mesenchyme, we generated and analyzed mandibular development in Smoc/c;Hand2-Cre mice, in which Cre expressed from the Hand2-Cre transgene is activated in post-migratory neural crest cells in the distal halves of the mandibular and other pharyngeal arches (Ruest et al., 2003).
evidence: The manuscript describes the Cre expression pattern with citation to previous study.

claim: Cre expressed from the Hand2-Cre transgene starts to be active after E9.0 and is restricted in the mandibular and other pharyngeal arches.
source: By crossing the Hand2-Cre transgenic mice with the R26R-lacZ Cre reporter mouse line (Soriano, 1999) and analyzing LacZ activity in the R26R-lacZ;Hand2-Cre embryos, we confirmed that Cre expressed from the Hand2-Cre transgene starts to be active after E9.0 and is restricted in the mandibular and other pharyngeal arches (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports lineage tracing results with reference to figures and cites the reporter mouse line.

claim: From E10.5 to E12.5, the Hand2-Cre lineage cells contribute to about the distal two thirds of the mandibular mesenchyme, including neural crest-derived mesenchyme in the developing tongue.
source: From E10.5 to E12.5, the Hand2-Cre lineage cells contribute to about the distal two thirds of the mandibular mesenchyme, including neural crest-derived mesenchyme in the developing tongue (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B–D,F–H), similar to previous findings (Ruest et al., 2003; Ruest et al., 2004).
evidence: The manuscript reports lineage tracing results with reference to figures and cites previous studies.

claim: Expression of Bmp4 mRNAs was similarly restricted to the distal mandibular ectoderm in the Smoc/c control and Smoc/c;Hand2-Cre mutant embryos at E10.5.
source: As shown in Figure 5, whereas expression of Bmp4 mRNAs was similarly restricted to the distal mandibular ectoderm in the Smoc/c control and Smoc/c;Hand2-Cre mutant embryos at E10.5 (Figure 5A,B), the pattern of expression of Msx1, Msx2, and Alx4, is each expanded to the oropharyngeal side of the distal mandibular arch mesenchyme in the Smoc/c;Hand2-Cre mutant embryos compared with the Smoc/c control embryos (Figure 5C–H).
evidence: The manuscript reports in situ hybridization results comparing control and mutant embryos with reference to figures.

claim: The pattern of expression of Msx1, Msx2, and Alx4 is each expanded to the oropharyngeal side of the distal mandibular arch mesenchyme in the Smoc/c;Hand2-Cre mutant embryos compared with the Smoc/c control embryos.
source: As shown in Figure 5, whereas expression of Bmp4 mRNAs was similarly restricted to the distal mandibular ectoderm in the Smoc/c control and Smoc/c;Hand2-Cre mutant embryos at E10.5 (Figure 5A,B), the pattern of expression of Msx1, Msx2, and Alx4, is each expanded to the oropharyngeal side of the distal mandibular arch mesenchyme in the Smoc/c;Hand2-Cre mutant embryos compared with the Smoc/c control embryos (Figure 5C–H).
evidence: The manuscript reports in situ hybridization results comparing control and mutant embryos with reference to figures.

claim: E10.5 control embryos exhibited a gradient distribution of pSmad1/5/9 positive cells, with the highest level in the mandibular mesenchyme immediately underlying the Bmp4-expressing mandibular ectoderm and the lowest level at the pharyngeal side.
source: Furthermore, we found by immunofluorescent staining that phosphorylated Smad1/5/9 (pSmad1/5/9) positive cells exhibit a gradient distribution, with the highest level in the mandibular mesenchyme immediately underlying the Bmp4-expressing mandibular ectoderm and the lowest level at the pharyngeal side of the mandibular arch mesenchyme, in E10.5 control embryos, but the E10.5 Smoc/c;Hand2-Cre mutant embryos exhibited high levels of pSmad1/5/9 throughout the oral-aboral axis of the distal mandibular arch mesenchyme (Figure 5I–K).
evidence: The manuscript reports immunofluorescence staining results with reference to figures.

claim: E10.5 Smoc/c;Hand2-Cre mutant embryos exhibited high levels of pSmad1/5/9 throughout the oral-aboral axis of the distal mandibular arch mesenchyme.
source: Furthermore, we found by immunofluorescent staining that phosphorylated Smad1/5/9 (pSmad1/5/9) positive cells exhibit a gradient distribution, with the highest level in the mandibular mesenchyme immediately underlying the Bmp4-expressing mandibular ectoderm and the lowest level at the pharyngeal side of the mandibular arch mesenchyme, in E10.5 control embryos, but the E10.5 Smoc/c;Hand2-Cre mutant embryos exhibited high levels of pSmad1/5/9 throughout the oral-aboral axis of the distal mandibular arch mesenchyme (Figure 5I–K).
evidence: The manuscript reports immunofluorescence staining results with reference to figures.

claim: Smoc/c;Hand2-Cre embryos had a shortened mandible but their skull and upper jaw were mostly unaffected.
source: Skeletal preparations of E18.5 embryos showed that the Smoc/c;Hand2-Cre embryos had a shortened mandible but their skull and upper jaw were mostly unaffected, in comparison with the control littermates (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: The manuscript reports skeletal analysis results from mutant mice with reference to figures.

claim: Smoc/c;Hand2-Cre embryos displayed severe defect in tongue formation although they had normal development of the nasal and upper jaw structures, including normal development of the secondary palate.
source: Histological analysis showed that the Smoc/c;Hand2-Cre embryos displayed severe defect in tongue formation although they had normal development of the nasal and upper jaw structures, including normal development of the secondary palate (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: The manuscript reports histological analysis results from mutant mice with reference to figures.

claim: Myf5-expressing tongue muscle precursor cells arriving at the mandibular arch in the E10.5 Smoc/c;Hand2-Cre embryos were significantly reduced compared with the control littermates.
source: Similar to that reported in Smoc/n;Wnt1-Cre embryos (Jeong et al., 2004), Myf5-expressing tongue muscle precursor cells arriving at the mandibular arch in the E10.5 Smoc/c;Hand2-Cre embryos were significantly reduced compared with the control littermates (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: The manuscript reports in situ hybridization results with reference to figures and cites previous study.

claim: At E15.5, the Smoc/c;Hand2-Cre mutant embryos displayed a cleft and rudimentary tongue in the pharyngeal region and absence of oral part of the tongue.
source: At E15.5, the Smoc/c;Hand2-Cre mutant embryos displayed a cleft and rudimentary tongue in the pharyngeal region and absence of oral part of the tongue (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C–H).
evidence: The manuscript reports histological analysis results from mutant mice with reference to figures.

claim: Smoc/c;Hand2-Cre mutant embryos exhibited ectopic ossification in the oral side of the mandibular mesenchyme as early as E12.5.
source: Analysis of expression of Runx2 and alkaline phosphatase on coronal sections showed that the Smoc/c;Hand2-Cre mutant embryos exhibited ectopic ossification in the oral side of the mandibular mesenchyme as early as E12.5 (Figure 6E–H).
evidence: The manuscript reports histological analysis results from mutant mice with reference to figures.

claim: Inactivation of Smo in the neural crest cells either prior to their migration into the mandibular arch or after their arrival in the mandibular arch led to similar disruption of mandibular structures, including disruption of tongue formation and ectopic bone formation from the oral side of the mandibular arch mesenchyme.
source: These results indicate that inactivation of Smo in the neural crest cells either prior to their migration into the mandibular arch, as in Smoc/c;Wnt1-Cre embryos, or after their arrival in the mandibular arch, as in Smoc/c;Hand2-Cre embryos, led to similar disruption of mandibular structures, including disruption of tongue formation and ectopic bone formation from the oral side of the mandibular arch mesenchyme.
evidence: The manuscript provides an interpretation comparing phenotypes of different mutant mice.

claim: Hedgehog signaling in the neural crest-derived mandibular mesenchyme is crucial for inducing tongue formation and preventing osteogenic differentiation in the oral side of the developing mandible.
source: Together, these results indicate that hedgehog signaling in the neural crest-derived mandibular mesenchyme is crucial for inducing tongue formation and preventing osteogenic differentiation in the oral side of the developing mandible.
evidence: The manuscript provides an interpretation of the observed phenotypes in mutant mice.

claim: Expression of Foxf1 is activated throughout the oral-aboral axis of the distal mandibular arch mesenchyme in E10.5 R26SmoM2;Hand2-Cre embryos.
source: As shown in Figure 7, expression of Foxf1, a known direct transcriptional target gene downstream of hedgehog signaling (Hoffmann et al., 2014), is activated throughout the oral-aboral axis of the distal mandibular arch mesenchyme in E10.5 R26SmoM2;Hand2-Cre embryos, in comparison with the restricted expression of Foxf1 at the oropharyngeal side of the mandibular arch mesenchyme in control littermates (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: The manuscript reports in situ hybridization results with reference to figures and cites previous study.

claim: Expression of Msx2 and Alx4 in the distal mandibular arch mesenchyme is significantly reduced in the E10.5 R26SmoM2;Hand2-Cre mouse embryos compared with control littermates.
source: Compared with the control littermates, expression of Msx2 and Alx4 in the distal mandibular arch mesenchyme is significantly reduced in the E10.5 R26SmoM2;Hand2-Cre mouse embryos (Figure 7C–F).
evidence: The manuscript reports in situ hybridization results comparing control and mutant embryos with reference to figures.

claim: E10.5 R26SmoM2;Hand2-Cre embryos showed a significant decrease in the number of pSmad1/5/9 positive cells in the distal mandibular arch mesenchyme compared with control littermates.
source: Furthermore, immunofluorescent staining of sagittal sections of E10.5 embryos showed a significant decrease in the number of pSmad1/5/9 positive cells in the distal mandibular arch mesenchyme of E10.5 R26SmoM2;Hand2-Cre embryos compared with control littermates (Figure 7G–I).
evidence: The manuscript reports immunofluorescence staining results with reference to figures.

claim: Hedgehog-Smo signaling regulates BMP signaling pathway activation along the oral-aboral axis in the mandibular arch mesenchyme.
source: These results confirm that hedgehog-Smo signaling regulates BMP signaling pathway activation along the oral-aboral axis in the mandibular arch mesenchyme.
evidence: The manuscript provides an interpretation of the observed gene expression and signaling changes.

claim: Blocking Smo-mediated hedgehog signaling causes increased apoptosis of the neural crest cells in the developing facial primordia in both chick and mouse embryos.
source: Previous studies showed that blocking Smo-mediated hedgehog signaling causes increased apoptosis of the neural crest cells in the developing facial primordia in both chick and mouse embryos (Ahlgren and Bronner-Fraser, 1999; Hu and Helms, 1999; Jeong et al., 2004).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies reporting apoptosis in response to hedgehog signaling disruption.

claim: The truncation of the maxillary and mandibular structures in Smoc/n;Wnt1-Cre mutant mice was partly attributed to increased apoptosis of neural crest cells in the mutant facial primordia at E9.5 to E10.5.
source: The truncation of the maxillary and mandibular structures in Smoc/n;Wnt1-Cre mutant mice was partly attributed to increased apoptosis of neural crest cells in the mutant facial primordia at E9.5 to E10.5 (Jeong et al., 2004).
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study attributing phenotypes to apoptosis.

claim: No increase in apoptosis was detectable in E9.5 Smoc/c;Hand2-Cre embryos.
source: Whereas no increase in apoptosis was detectable in E9.5 Smoc/c;Hand2-Cre embryos, we detected a group of cells with strong Caspase-3 activity specifically in the distal mandibular arch mesenchyme in E10.5 Smoc/c;Hand2-Cre embryos (Figure 8A,B).
evidence: The manuscript reports apoptosis analysis results with reference to figures.

claim: A group of cells with strong Caspase-3 activity was detected specifically in the distal mandibular arch mesenchyme in E10.5 Smoc/c;Hand2-Cre embryos.
source: Whereas no increase in apoptosis was detectable in E9.5 Smoc/c;Hand2-Cre embryos, we detected a group of cells with strong Caspase-3 activity specifically in the distal mandibular arch mesenchyme in E10.5 Smoc/c;Hand2-Cre embryos (Figure 8A,B).
evidence: The manuscript reports apoptosis analysis results with reference to figures.

claim: The increased apoptosis in the distal mandibular mesenchyme correlated with the distal truncation of both the dentary bone on the aboral side and the ectopic bone on the oral side of the mutant mandible.
source: The increased apoptosis in the distal mandibular mesenchyme correlated with the distal truncation of both the dentary bone on the aboral side and the ectopic bone on the oral side of the mutant mandible (Figure 8E,F).
evidence: The manuscript describes correlation between apoptosis and skeletal phenotypes with reference to figures.

claim: Increased BMP signaling has been correlated with increased neural crest apoptosis in mouse embryos lacking both Noggin and Chordin.
source: Since we detected expanded activation of pSmad1/5/9 and Bmp4 target gene expression in the mandibular arch mesenchyme in the E10.5 Smoc/c;Hand2-Cre mutant embryos and since increased BMP signaling has been correlated with increased neural crest apoptosis in mouse embryos lacking both Noggin and Chordin, two endogenous antagonists of BMPs (Anderson et al., 2006; Stottmann et al., 2001), we investigated whether reducing the Bmp4 gene dosage could rescue mandibular morphogenesis in the Smoc/c;Hand2-Cre embryos.
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies correlating BMP signaling with apoptosis.

claim: The amount of active caspase-3 positive cells was significantly reduced in the mandibular mesenchyme of E10.5 Smoc/c;Hand2-Cre;Bmp4+/- embryos in comparison with Smoc/c;Hand2-Cre littermates.
source: We found that the amount of active caspase-3 positive cells was significantly reduced in the mandibular mesenchyme of E10.5 Smoc/c;Hand2-Cre;Bmp4+/- embryos in comparison with Smoc/c;Hand2-Cre littermates (Figure 8B–D).
evidence: The manuscript reports apoptosis analysis results comparing different genotypes with reference to figures.

claim: 4 out of 5 Smoc/c;Hand2-Cre;Bmp4+/- mutants showed partial rescue of distal mandible and formation of the mandibular symphysis.
source: By E18.5, 4 out of 5 Smoc/c;Hand2-Cre;Bmp4+/- mutants showed partial rescue of distal mandible and formation of the mandibular symphysis, in contrast to the lack of distal mandibular skeletal structures in the Smoc/c;Hand2Cre mutants (Figure 8F,G).
evidence: The manuscript reports skeletal analysis results from genetic rescue experiments with reference to figures.

claim: Smoc/c;Hand2-Cre;Bmp4+/- pups still showed tongue agenesis and duplication of the dentary bone on the oral side.
source: However, the Smoc/c;Hand2-Cre;Bmp4+/- pups still showed tongue agenesis and duplication of the dentary bone on the oral side (Figure 8G).
evidence: The manuscript reports skeletal analysis results from genetic rescue experiments with reference to figures.

claim: Hedgehog signaling regulates mandibular arch mesenchyme survival and oral-aboral patterning through antagonizing BMP signaling.
source: These results indicate that hedgehog signaling regulates mandibular arch mesenchyme survival and oral-aboral patterning through antagonizing BMP signaling.
evidence: The manuscript provides an interpretation of the genetic rescue experiment results.

claim: Hedgehog signaling regulates expression of several members of the Fox gene family, including Foxf1 and Foxf2, in the developing mouse facial primordia.
source: It has been shown previously that hedgehog signaling regulates expression of several members of the Fox gene family, including Foxf1 and Foxf2, in the developing mouse facial primordia (Jeong et al., 2004).
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study reporting hedgehog regulation of Fox genes.

claim: Expression of Foxf1, Foxf2, and Ptch1 mRNAs was dramatically reduced in the distal mandibular arch mesenchyme in E10.5 Smoc/c;Hand2-Cre embryos compared with their control littermates.
source: We found that expression of Foxf1 and Foxf2, as well as Ptch1 mRNAs, was dramatically reduced in the distal mandibular arch mesenchyme in E10.5 Smoc/c;Hand2-Cre embryos compared with their control littermates (Figure 9A–F).
evidence: The manuscript reports in situ hybridization results comparing control and mutant embryos with reference to figures.

claim: Neural crest-specific inactivation of either Foxf1 or Foxf2 caused cleft palate but did not significantly affect mandible and tongue development.
source: We recently showed that neural crest-specific inactivation of either Foxf1 or Foxf2 caused cleft palate but did not significantly affect mandible and tongue development (Xu et al., 2016b).
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study by the authors reporting phenotypes of single gene knockouts.

claim: Foxf1c/c;Foxf2c/c;Wnt1-Cre mouse embryos exhibited absence of the oral tongue and ectopic ossification at the oral side of the mandibular mesenchyme.

claim: Neural crest cells in the dorsal portion of the first pharyngeal arch contribute to trabecular bones of the neural cranium.
source: As has been demonstrated by cell lineage studies in both axolotl and chick embryos, neural crest cells in the dorsal portion of the first pharyngeal arch contribute to trabecular bones of the neural cranium whereas neural crest cells in the ventral portion of the first arch, referred to as the mandibular arch, give rise to skeletal elements of both the upper and lower jaws (Cerny et al., 2004; Kuratani et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous lineage tracing studies.

claim: Neural crest cells in the ventral portion of the first arch, referred to as the mandibular arch, give rise to skeletal elements of both the upper and lower jaws.
